explain.say: Want to say hello in Spanish, Japanese or Swahili? Good news: little and often beats long and rare. Look at the checklist on the board. First tick: listen a little every day, a song, a cartoon or a short video. Your ears learn the music of the language first.

explain.say: Now look at this curve on the board. It shows how fast we forget: very fast at first! But see the marks? Each time you review a word, just before you forget it, the memory gets stronger and lasts longer.

That trick is called spaced repetition: reviewing at bigger and bigger gaps. See the fourth tick on the checklist? Review old words. Flashcards or an app can remind you when. How could you make flashcards at home?

faq.a: Spaced repetition means reviewing a word just before you are likely to forget it, then waiting longer each time: a day, a few days, a week, a month.

faq.q: How do I remember new words?
faq.a: Use them in your own sentences, say them out loud, link them to pictures, and review them with spaced repetition.
Listen to songs, cartoons, podcasts or videos in the language for a few minutes every day. Subtitles in the same language help a lot.

faq.q: How do I find someone to practise with?
faq.a: Try family members, classmates, a language club, a teacher, or a pen pal programme run by your school. Always ask a parent or carer before talking to anyone online.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn a language?
faq.a: It depends on the language and how much you practise. A few minutes daily lets you chat simply within months, but getting fluent takes years, and that is normal.
asks: How fast can I become fluent?

facts: The forgetting curve was first measured by German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus in 1885.
Short daily practice is usually better for memory than one long session a week.
